story.title: Lindsay Clancy Scheduled for Retrial in March 2027 for Children's Deaths
story.summary: Lindsay Clancy is set to face a retrial on March 29, 2027, regarding the deaths of her three children, following a previous trial that ended in a mistrial due to a jury deadlock. Prosecutors are pursuing murder charges, while Clancy's defense claims she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the incident.

explore_lenses.label: Why is criminal responsibility the central issue?
explore_lenses.title: The acts are not the main dispute
explore_lenses.summary: The first trial focused on whether Clancy was legally criminally responsible at the time of the children’s deaths, rather than on whether she caused them. The deadlock showed that jurors sharply disagreed on that question.

claims.text: Clancy has not disputed that she killed her three children in Duxbury in January 2023; her lawyers have argued that postpartum psychosis left her unable to control her behavior.
Prosecutors have acknowledged mental-health problems but argue that Clancy acted deliberately and understood that her actions were wrong.
Eleven jurors favored finding Clancy not criminally responsible on insanity grounds, while one juror disagreed, so the jury could not reach the unanimous verdict required.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: A second jury may assess the same evidence differently; the first jury’s split was not a verdict.

explore_lenses.label: Why was a retrial allowed after the mistrial?
explore_lenses.title: The judge rejected the double-jeopardy challenge
explore_lenses.summary: Clancy’s defense argued that the court should not have declared a mistrial after the jury deadlocked. Judge William Sullivan ruled that the deadlock made a mistrial necessary, permitting another prosecution on the murder indictments.

claims.text: The defense sought dismissal on the ground that the court should have removed the juror favoring conviction and allowed deliberations to continue.
Sullivan held that the deadlock created a “manifest necessity” for a mistrial and that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s protection against double jeopardy.
Sullivan also concluded that probing the jury’s deliberations or granting the requested juror-related records would improperly intrude on jury secrecy and was not material to a retrial.

explore_lenses.label: What remains to be decided before March?
explore_lenses.title: The exact prosecution strategy is still not public
explore_lenses.summary: The court set March 29, 2027, for the new trial and scheduled a December hearing on logistics. Prosecutors signaled that they want a jury trial, but the district attorney had not publicly specified the final charges as of November 16.

claims.text: Judge Sullivan set the retrial for March 29, 2027, after prosecutors requested a later May date because of scheduling conflicts.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court on December 30, 2026, to address trial logistics, security and media arrangements.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors were ready to select a jury-trial date; defense lawyer Kevin Reddington interpreted that as an indication prosecutors intend to proceed on first-degree murder charges.
The Plymouth County district attorney had not publicly confirmed whether the retrial would use the same first-degree murder charges or different charges.

story_report.summary: Lindsay Clancy is scheduled to be retried on March 29, 2027, after her first trial over the deaths of her three children ended in a mistrial because jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict. Prosecutors are seeking a murder conviction, while Clancy’s lawyers contend that postpartum psychosis left her unable to control her behavior. The retrial will give a new jury the task of assessing competing accounts of her mental state and intent.

sections.heading: First Jury Deadlocked on Insanity
sections.body: Clancy has not disputed killing her three children in Duxbury in January 2023. According to accounts of the first trial, 11 jurors favored finding her not criminally responsible by reason of insanity, while one juror disagreed, preventing the unanimous decision required. Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental-health problems but argued that she acted deliberately and knew her actions were wrong.

sections.heading: Judge Sullivan Rejects Dismissal Request
sections.body: The defense sought dismissal, arguing that the court should have removed the juror who favored conviction and permitted deliberations to continue. Judge Sullivan ruled that the deadlock created a “manifest necessity” for a mistrial and that trying Clancy again would not violate double-jeopardy protections. Sullivan also found that further inquiry into deliberations and the requested juror-related records would improperly intrude on jury secrecy and would not be material to a retrial.

sections.heading: Retrial Planning Continues Before March
sections.body: Sullivan set the March 29 date after prosecutors sought a May trial date because of scheduling conflicts. Attorneys are due back in court on December 30, 2026, to address trial logistics, security and media arrangements. Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors were ready to select a jury-trial date; defense lawyer Kevin Reddington said he took that as a sign prosecutors intend to pursue first-degree murder charges.

unresolved.text: The Plymouth County district attorney had not publicly confirmed whether the retrial will proceed on the same first-degree murder charges or different charges, and the final charging decision and each side’s trial presentation have not been publicly detailed.

The defense has said it plans to appeal the dismissal ruling, though it has said the appeal will not delay the retrial. A second jury may assess the evidence differently; the earlier split was not a verdict.

related_stories.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced the disbandment of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a unit that has faced criticism for its role in policing protests. This decision has drawn condemnation from police union leaders, who argue that it jeopardizes public safety.

related_stories.title: Seventeen Dead in Two Mass Shootings in South Africa
related_stories.summary: Seventeen people were killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, occurring in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. The first incident involved six men and three women found shot dead inside a shack near Pretoria. Police have not yet established motives for the shootings, which took place approximately 530 kilometers apart.
